verdict.root_cause: No investigated service is confirmed as origin; the one signal that survives scrutiny points inward at frontend. In all 10 sampled traces, frontend handler spans carry their duration as self-time (~4-7ms, one ~55ms outlier) with no child spans, while the outbound edges that appear (productcatalogservice/GetProduct, cartservice/GetCart with Redis HGET) return in single-digit ms with no error status [tr_82279b161d2a]. Frontend's own error ratio fell to about a fifth of baseline, so nothing is failing loudly downstream [tr_d18ea2b81967]. productcatalogservice is a co-symptom: its errors are only 1.22x its four-hour baseline and the 22:31 excursion is matched at 19:00 and 19:07 [tr_90363d0ff249], the zero-to-1.1% jump being an artifact of a short error-free baseline [tr_bf8410dff58c]. adservice memory-limit cycling is routine automation whose capped state ended ~1.9h before onset [tr_20ac9b3ec41c]. The failure is latency local to frontend's own processing, but no frontend latency-percentile, resource, or change data was ever retrieved, so the mechanism is unestablished.
verdict.reasoning: Traces localize the degrading hop to frontend self-time with clean, fast downstream edges [tr_82279b161d2a], which rules out inherited dependency latency on the sampled edges. Frontend error ratio moving down [tr_d18ea2b81967] rules out a hard-error propagation story. The productcatalogservice signal that co-alerted is within its own historical variability once a four-hour baseline is used [tr_90363d0ff249], undercutting the narrow-window jump [tr_bf8410dff58c]. No change record exists for productcatalogservice [tr_58c274c424c7] and adservice's limit churn was not in effect at onset [tr_20ac9b3ec41c]. What is missing is any frontend-side resource, latency-percentile, or change evidence, so the mechanism inside frontend cannot be named.
open_questions: No frontend CPU/memory/thread/GC or latency-percentile series was ever queried; frontend resource exhaustion remains untested.
No change history was queried for frontend, so a deploy or config edit on it is neither supported nor excluded.
The productcatalogservice log query used a mismatched label selector [tr_bc86f5cbbc83], so its logs are effectively unread; two of frontend's four outbound edges never appeared in the trace sample.
One unmeasured edge from triage was never crossed, and loadgenerator's simultaneous alert was not investigated.

alternatives.root_cause: Frontend ran out of CPU, threads, or heap, so requests queued inside its own handler and showed as self-time.
alternatives.why_not: Consistent with the self-time pattern, but no frontend resource or saturation metric was ever retrieved — the mechanism is inferred, not observed.

alternatives.root_cause: productcatalogservice began emitting intermittent errors around 22:31 and is the true origin, with frontend merely noticing.
alternatives.why_not: Its error rise vanishes against a four-hour baseline, sampled GetProduct calls are sub-2ms and error-free, and no change or log evidence supports a state change.

proposal.expected_effect: No action is proposed, so no change in any series is expected. The observable that would justify a later action does not yet exist in this investigation: frontend has no latency-percentile series (p50/p95/p99 on its HTTP handler), no CPU/memory/thread/GC series, and no change-history record retrieved. Those three queries are the next step, not a remediation.
proposal.if_wrong: This abstention is wrong if someone produces evidence meeting a precondition I do not currently see: (a) a frontend change-history entry naming a deploy, image, or config edit inside the 22:03-22:35 window, which would make rollback_image or revert_config eligible; or (b) a frontend resource/GC series showing saturation or a restart-count pattern, which would make restart_service eligible as process-state evidence. Absent either, every permitted action is a guess. Note also that the only latency signal here is 10 sampled traces with one ~55ms outlier [tr_82279b161d2a] and no percentile series at all - so even the symptom I would be treating is unquantified, and I could not tell after a restart whether it had improved.
proposal.risk: The risk of abstaining is that frontend-local latency persists and user-visible slowness continues unremediated for the length of one more query round. The risk of the action I am declining is larger and asymmetric: restart_service on frontend is marked irreversible and discards in-process cache, so a cold frontend would likely make the very self-time latency in [tr_82279b161d2a] worse for minutes while caches refill, and with no pre-restart percentile baseline nobody could distinguish recovery from further degradation. It would also destroy the process state that is the only remaining place the unestablished mechanism could be read from.
proposal.blast_radius: None from this proposal. For context on what was declined: frontend is the edge service in this blast radius, taking traffic from loadgenerator (itself alerted) and fanning out to productcatalogservice, cartservice, adservice and, transitively, checkoutservice and recommendationservice. A frontend recreate resets connections for every loadgenerator request in flight and is the one service in this graph whose interruption is directly user-visible; the downstream services would see their inbound traffic stop and resume rather than error.
proposal._notes: productcatalogservice is explicitly ruled out as origin [tr_90363d0ff249, tr_bf8410dff58c] and adservice's memory cycling had ended ~1.9h before onset [tr_20ac9b3ec41c], so neither is a legitimate target either. Its logs are effectively unread due to a label mismatch [tr_bc86f5cbbc83], but re-reading them is an investigation step, not a remediation.

triage_judgement.reasoning: Critical severity with simultaneous alerts on frontend, productcatalogservice, and the load generator indicates a real user-facing failure, not a single quiet latency warning. No open incidents to attribute it to, and the simultaneity leaves the origin ambiguous between a catalog-side fault and a shared dependency.
